SECTION - A (Conventional Type) (34 Marks)
This Section should be answered only on the Answer Sheet provided.
Marks for each question is indicated against it.
1. Write a precis of the following passage, giving it a suitable title:
(14)
Communication is an essential requirement for all human performance and interaction. It
welds individuals into groups by developing common interests, by crystallising common concepts, by
establishing relationships, by extending cooperation, by sharing experience and by establishing a
common heritage. The underlying principle of each of these acts is that we use language as a means of
communication. In a much broader sense, language is a tool of communication, but aside from language,
there is also another important, but often overlooked means of communication.
When we talk about language as a means of communication, we mean the usage of language
and words– how they sound, how they are formed, their meaning, and their structure. However, we
do not use just words or language to communicate. Non-verbal communication– our body movements,
our expressions and our gestures - convey so much more than we are aware of. In fact, it is often said
that a person may lie with their words, but their bodies reveal the truth. When someone’s body
language is inconsistent with their words, we tend to believe the body language rather than the words.
Thus, both these means of communication– verbal and non-verbal, are both essential in effective
communication.
For example, a person may say that they are interested in what we are talking about, but if
they fidget constantly, or their eyes keep darting away, or their legs are angled away from us, their
body movements convey that they are either distracted, or they are not interested in what we have to
say. This is why, to excel in communication, it is important to focus on both what we are saying, but
on what our bodies are conveying. A pleasant facial expression, open gestures, and correct posture
suggests that you are confident, honest and invested in what you are trying to express. No matter the
content of the speech, if the speaker just drones on without making eye contact with the audience, or
he crosses his arms, the audience will find it hard to fully connect with him or what he is saying. The
most effective communication, therefore, incorporates the skillful usage of both verbal and non-verbal
means of communication.

2. Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follow:-
From the wealth of science we have selected certain parts. And our choice has in no way
been influenced by a consideration of the higher interest of humanity. It has simply followed the path
of our natural tendencies. The principles of the greatest convenience and of the least effort, the
pleasure to be had from speed, change, and comfort, and also the burning need of escaping from
ourselves, are the driving force in the success of new inventions. But no one has ever stopped to ask
how we would cope with the enormous acceleration of the pace of life resulting from rapid
transportation, telegraph, telephone, modern business methods, machines that write and calculate,
and those that do all the housekeeping drudgery of former times. Steam-heated houses, electric
lighting, elevators, and the chemical doctoring and adulteration of foodstuffs have been accepted
lock, stock, and barrel, their comprehensive adoption being solely precipitated by the hedonic and
facilitative advantages they confer. Nevertheless, no account whatsoever has been taken of their
probable effect on human beings.
In the organization of industrial life, the influence of the factory upon the physiological and
mental state of the workers has been left by the wayside. Modern industry is based on the conception
of the maximum production at lowest cost so that an individual or a group of individuals may rake in
as much money as possible. It has expanded without any idea of the true nature of the human beings
who run the machines, and without giving a second thought to the effect produced on the individuals
and on their descendants by the artificial mode of existence imposed by the factory. The great cities
have been built with no regard for us. The shape and dimensions of the skyscrapers hinge entirely on
the necessity of obtaining the maximum income per square foot of ground, and of offering to the
tenants’ offices and apartments that please them. This caused the construction of gigantic buildings
where far too many human beings are crammed together. Civilized men have a taste for such a way of
living. While they soak up the comfort and banal luxury of their dwelling, they do not realise that they
are missing out on the necessities of life. A modern city consists of monstrous edifices and of dark,
narrow streets chock-full of gasoline fumes, coal dust and toxic gases, shattered by the noise of the
taxi cabs, trucks, and trolleys, and swarming ceaselessly with great crowds. Obviously, it has not
been planned for the good of its inhabitants.
Our life is influenced to a great extent by commercial advertising. Such publicity is undertaken
purely and simply in the interest of the advertisers and not of the consumers. For example, the public
has been hoodwinked into believing that white bread is better than brown. Consequently, flour has
been treated more and more thoroughly and thus stripped of its most useful components. Such
treatment allows for its preservation for longer periods and facilitates the making of bread. The
millers and the bakers line their pockets. The consumers eat an inferior product, under the impression
that it is a superior one. And in the countries where bread is the principal food, the population goes
downhill. Enormous amounts of money are poured into publicity. As a result, large quantities of
pharmaceutical products that are at the least useless, and often harmful, have become the norm for
civilized men. In this manner, the raw greed of individuals sufficiently shrewd to whip up a popular
demand for the goods that they have for sale calls the shots in the modern world.
(i) According to the passage, why have modern inventions and industrial developments been widely
adopted without considering their effects on human beings?
(2)
(ii) Why does the author criticize modern industry’s approach to production?
(2)
(iii) According to the passage, what role does greed play in the modern world?
(2)
(iv) What is the meaning of the phrase ‘accepted lock, stock, and barrel’ used in the passage?
(2)
(a) Accepted slowly and tentatively.
(b) Accepted with minor alterations and exceptions.
(c) Accepted completely, including all its parts or details.
(d) Accepted only the beneficial parts of the innovation.

- 3 -
(v) What is the meaning of the idiom ‘calls the shots’ in the final paragraph?
(2)
(a) To make suggestions or give advice.
(b) To receive orders from a higher authority.
(c) To be the person or group in control and making the decisions.
(d) To publicly advertise products and services.
3. Imagine you’re the Child Development Project Officer (CDPO) of a Rural Development Block. You
have recently conducted a survey and found a significant increase in malnutrition among children aged
0-5. Draft a formal letter to the Director, Women & Child Development, outlining the urgent need for
a special nutritional supplement program in your Block. In the letter, detail the key findings of your
survey, propose specific actions to address the issue, and request the allocation of necessary funds
and resources.
(10)

Direction (Question Nos. 32 - 36): Choose the correct option and change the following sentences as
directed:
32. The maid said, “The boy was hiding in a closet.” (to Indirect)
(a) The maid said that the boy was hiding in a closet.
(b) The maid said that the boy hid in a closet
(c) The maid said that the boy had been hiding in a closet.
(d) The maid said that the boy had hid in a closet.
33. He told me that he had not seen Mary since the previous day. (to Direct)
(a) He told me, “I had not seen Mary since the previous day.”
(b) He said to me, “I have not seen Mary since yesterday.”
(c) He tells to me “I had not seen Mary since the previous day.”
(d) He said, “He had not seen Mary since the previous day.”
34. She said to Peter, “Give me your book, please” (to Indirect)
(a) She said to Peter that give her his book please.
(b) She requested Peter to give her his book.
(c) She told Peter to give her his book please.
(d) She asked Peter to give me your book.
35. The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun. (to Direct)
(a) The teacher said, “The earth revolves around the sun.”
(b) The teacher said, “the earth revolved around the sun.”
(c) The teacher says, “The earth revolve around the sun.”
(d) The teacher said, “The earth has revolved around the sun.”
36. Siami said, “Rama called me up this morning.” (to Indirect)
(a) Siami said that Rama called me up this morning.
(b) Siami said that Rama called her up this morning.
(c) Siami said that Rama called her up that morning.
(d) Siami said that Rama had called her up that morning.
